title: Type casting (the four cast operators)
relevance: Interviewers use C++ cast operators to check whether candidates express conversion intent clearly and choose the safe cast for downcasting, const, and low-level reinterpretation.

phases.goal: Establish why C-style casts are unsafe and what each of the four named cast operators is for.

must_hit.point: A C-style cast is dangerous because it is permissive, does not state intent, silently picks whichever conversion compiles, and is hard to search for.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says C-style casts hide intent and can perform unexpected conversions that are hard to grep.

must_hit.point: Modern C++ provides four named cast operators—static_cast, dynamic_cast, const_cast, and reinterpret_cast—each expressing a single specific intent and searchable in code.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all four operators and contrasts them with the single C-style syntax.

must_hit.point: C++ still supports C-style (Type)expression and functional Type(expression) casts, but they should be avoided in modern C++.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions both old forms and recommends avoiding them entirely.

probes: Why prefer the named cast operators over a C-style cast?

hints.1: Think about what a C-style cast communicates versus what the compiler allows.
hints.2: Compare one terse syntax that can do many conversions with operators that each name one intent.
hints.3: C-style casts are hard to search, hide intent, and can silently act as const_cast, static_cast, or reinterpret_cast until one compiles.

phases.goal: Explain how each named cast works, including RTTI requirements and failure behavior for dynamic_cast.

must_hit.point: static_cast does compile-time checked conversions between related types: numeric conversions, upcasting, explicit downcasting without a run-time check, void* to typed pointer, and forcing an explicit constructor or conversion operator.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists several static_cast uses and notes downcasting assumes you know the real type.

must_hit.point: dynamic_cast does safe run-time checked polymorphic downcasting using RTTI; it requires a polymorphic type (base has at least one virtual function), returns nullptr for failed pointer casts, and throws std::bad_cast for failed reference casts.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties dynamic_cast to RTTI/vtable, polymorphism, nullptr vs bad_cast.

must_hit.point: const_cast is the only cast that can add or remove const or volatile qualifiers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States exclusivity for cv-qualifier changes, often for legacy non-const APIs.

must_hit.point: reinterpret_cast reinterprets bits between unrelated pointer or integer types without data conversion; behaviour is largely implementation-defined and non-portable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes bit-pattern reinterpretation for systems/hardware/allocator work, not a value conversion.

must_hit.point: RTTI tracks dynamic types at run time and also provides typeid (in <typeinfo>), which yields a std::type_info for the run-time type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines RTTI and mentions typeid alongside dynamic_cast.

probes: What is the difference between static_cast and dynamic_cast?

hints.1: Start with when each cast is checked: compile time versus run time.
hints.2: For downcasts, contrast blind trust versus asking the run-time system via the vtable.
hints.3: static_cast is compile-time and fast but unsafe if the actual type is wrong; dynamic_cast uses RTTI on a polymorphic type and returns nullptr or throws on failure.

phases.goal: Compare when to use each cast and why C-style casts obscure the intended conversion.

must_hit.point: Prefer static_cast for well-defined safe conversions or to reverse an implicit conversion; prefer dynamic_cast when you need a run-time-checked polymorphic downcast.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps static_cast to intended related-type conversions and dynamic_cast to safely querying a derived type.

must_hit.point: A C-style cast silently tries const_cast, then static_cast, then reinterpret_cast until one compiles, which can mask bugs when only a static_cast was intended.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the silent fallback sequence and why it obscures intent.

must_hit.point: reinterpret_cast is reserved for low-level systems work (hardware, custom allocators) because it is inherently dangerous compared with the more constrained named casts.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says use it sparingly for raw bit/pointer reinterpretation, not routine conversions.

probes: When would you choose dynamic_cast over static_cast for a downcast?

hints.1: Ask whether you need a run-time check that the object really is the derived type.
hints.2: static_cast assumes you are sure; dynamic_cast verifies via RTTI on a polymorphic hierarchy.
hints.3: Use dynamic_cast when safety matters and you can handle nullptr or std::bad_cast; use static_cast only when the type is certain and you accept no run-time check.

phases.goal: Apply the casts to safe downcasting, legacy APIs, and recognizing undefined or compile-time failure cases.

must_hit.point: Safely downcast with dynamic_cast on a pointer and check whether the result is nullptr before using the derived interface.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows pointer dynamic_cast plus a null check, contrasting with reference casts that throw.

must_hit.point: Use const_cast to pass const data into legacy C APIs that take non-const pointers but do not actually modify the data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the legacy API interop pattern as the typical const_cast use.

must_hit.point: dynamic_cast on a hierarchy with no virtual functions is a compile-time error; the base typically needs a virtual destructor to be polymorphic.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the polymorphic requirement and virtual destructor habit.

probes: What goes wrong if you const_cast away const and then modify an object that was originally declared const?

hints.1: For downcasting, prefer the cast that can report failure at run time.
hints.2: Use dynamic_cast to a pointer and test for nullptr; for const, only strip const if the object is truly mutable.
hints.3: Safe path: dynamic_cast<Derived*>(basePtr) then null-check; modifying after stripping const from an originally const object is undefined behaviour.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: static_cast does compile-time conversions with no run-time overhead, so it is fast but unsafe for downcasting if the actual type is wrong. dynamic_cast does a safe RTTI-checked polymorphic downcast, returning nullptr or throwing std::bad_cast on failure, and requires a polymorphic class.

Named casts each express one intent and let the compiler enforce rules. A C-style cast silently attempts const_cast, then static_cast, then reinterpret_cast until one compiles, masking bugs and obscuring intent.
Failed pointer dynamic_cast returns nullptr; failed reference dynamic_cast throws std::bad_cast because there is no null reference.

gotchas.trap: Using dynamic_cast on a class hierarchy with no virtual functions.
gotchas.correction: That is a compile-time error; the base must be polymorphic (typically with a virtual destructor).

gotchas.trap: const_cast to strip const from an object originally declared const, then modifying it.
gotchas.correction: That is undefined behaviour; only cast away const if the underlying object is truly mutable.

gotchas.trap: Using static_cast for a downcast when the object's actual type might be wrong.
gotchas.correction: static_cast has no run-time check; use dynamic_cast when you need verification via RTTI.

gotchas.trap: Relying on a C-style cast when you only meant a static_cast.
gotchas.correction: It can silently degrade into const_cast or reinterpret_cast; use the named operator that matches your intent.
